title: Other Christians (CCC 838)
hookLine: Catholics recognize a real though imperfect communion with all the baptized

lines: OLD QUARRELS NONE OF THEM STARTED.
cards: Thanksgiving, and the turkey is late. The grandmother is Catholic. One son became a Baptist when he married.

A granddaughter goes to a Greek Orthodox church with her husband. A cousin is Lutheran. Around one table, four ways of being Christian, and old quarrels between their churches that none of them started.
Someone says grace, and there's a small pause while everyone decides whose words to use. What does the Catholic Church say about the people at the other end of that table?
Its answer is written down, and it's warmer than some of the guests expect.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: It starts with a prayer. The night before he died, Jesus prayed for his followers, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee."
Every division among Christians, Catholics say, runs against that prayer.
Ecumenism, from the Greek oikoumene, the whole inhabited world, is the work of Christians seeking the unity Jesus prayed for.
The Catechism teaches that the Church is joined in many ways to all the baptized who bear the name of Christian, even when they don't share the full Catholic faith or unity with the pope.

It calls this a real, though imperfect, communion. People born into other churches today, it says, can't be blamed for the old separations, and Catholics accept them with respect and affection as brothers and sisters.

Many elements of holiness and truth are found outside the Catholic Church's visible structure, and the Spirit uses them. Other Christians describe the relationship in their own words, and Catholics don't speak for them.
Then, what changed. In 1964 the Second Vatican Council issued a decree on ecumenism.
In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople lifted the excommunications Rome and Constantinople had exchanged in 1054.
Since then: joint statements, shared prayer, and, each January in many places, a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Unity isn't finished.
The Catechism says the work of seeking it belongs to the whole Church, every member and not just the clergy.

how: Catholics join other Christians each January 18–25 in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and many parishes share services, Bible studies and charitable work with neighboring churches.

o: a council of bishops from all over the world
Christians working toward the unity Jesus prayed for
merging every church into one under a single leader

games.q: it's December 1965. the pope in Rome and the patriarch in Constantinople issue one joint declaration, read in both cities. what does it do about the excommunications of 1054?
games.why: Paul VI and Athenagoras lifted the mutual excommunications, a first step, not a full reunion.

practice: Picture Christians you know from other churches, a Baptist neighbor, an Orthodox friend, a Pentecostal coworker, a Lutheran cousin, around one table, and if anything in you tightens, let it soften.
If you pray, you can use Jesus's own words, that they all may be one, holding each face as you say them. If you don't, simply hold the table in your mind, full.

wordCard.voice: Ecumenism. From the Greek for the whole inhabited world: the work of Christians seeking the unity Jesus prayed for. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the inhabited world, the root of ecumenical.

carryVoice: Your line: that they may be one. The quarrels are old, and nobody at that table started them. Day three hundred twenty, done.
